title: Evidence-informed design review for the Business Ethics adventure
extensionScope: Additional review requested for motivation, current student perspectives, informative feedback, co-design and integration of independent online play with classroom learning.
status: Design evidence review completed; this product has not undergone a student learning evaluation

searchScope.reviewType: Targeted critical literature review, not an exhaustive systematic review
searchScope.purpose: Translate relevant research into requirements for an adult browser adventure that teaches the complete existing curriculum from beginner level.
searchScope.preferredAccess: Publisher pages, author manuscripts and institutional research repositories; third-party summaries were used only to locate original records.
topics: Learning content integrated into game mechanics
searchScope.dateCoverage: Foundational evidence from 2003 onward plus focused searches for 2023-2026 work; papers published after the review date were not intentionally included.
queries: Alfieri discovery learning assisted explicit instruction meta-analysis
Atkinson Renkl fading worked examples self-explanation transfer
Chernikova simulation higher education salience authenticity
Business ethics serious games learning experiment 2025 2026
limitations: Search ranking can miss relevant literature, especially non-English and unpublished work.
Some records were available only as abstracts or institutional descriptions; these are identified separately.
The reviews overlap in primary studies and cannot be counted as independent replications.
Most simulation and escape-room evidence comes from healthcare or other subjects, rather than Dutch Business Ethics beginners.
No result establishes a scientifically perfect game format or guarantees superiority over this particular e-learning.

sources.title: Does Discovery-Based Instruction Enhance Learning?
sources.readDepth: Author institutional abstract and bibliographic record
sources.design: Two random-effects meta-analyses covering 164 studies; 580 unassisted-discovery comparisons and 360 assisted-discovery comparisons.
sources.population: Mixed ages, subjects and instructional settings.
sources.comparison: Unassisted discovery versus explicit instruction; enhanced discovery versus other instruction.
sources.outcomes: Learning performance; retention and transfer are not separated in the accessible abstract.
sources.findings: Unassisted discovery was disadvantaged relative to explicit teaching (d=-0.38). Assisted discovery was favored (d=0.30). Feedback, examples, scaffolds and elicited explanations matter.
sources.limitations: Heterogeneous interventions; moderator associations do not identify a universally optimal sequence. This does not require every lesson to start with a lecture.
sources.designImplication: Give beginners a short concept explanation and a worked case, followed by guided investigation and progressively independent application.
sources.evidenceWeight: Strong general direction; indirect for this game.

sources.title: Transitioning From Studying Examples to Solving Problems: Effects of Self-Explanation Prompts and Fading Worked-Out Steps
sources.readDepth: Author institutional abstract; detailed sample sizes and allocation were not verified from full text
sources.design: Two instructional experiments comparing worked-step fading and principle-focused self-explanation prompts.
sources.population: Learners studying structured problem solving; do not use this record to infer adult ethics-specific effects.
sources.comparison: Fading combined with prompts versus fading alone or example/problem procedures.
sources.outcomes: Near and far transfer; learning time.
sources.findings: Fading alone had less reliable far-transfer benefits. Combining fading with explanations of underlying principles improved near and far transfer without extra learning time.
sources.limitations: Two domain-specific experiments; structured problems differ from contested ethical reasoning. Long-term retention was not established in the accessible record.
sources.designImplication: First show a completed evidence-to-claim connection, then leave connections for the learner to finish and explain; finally remove the model on a changed case.
sources.evidenceWeight: Useful causal mechanism with limited domain generalization.

sources.title: The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes
sources.readDepth: Original author manuscript; definitions and evidence tables inspected
sources.design: Original explanatory framework with reanalysis and synthesis of experimental/classroom findings; not a meta-analysis.
sources.population: Multiple subjects, ages and learning activities.
sources.comparison: Passive, active, constructive and interactive forms of engagement.
sources.outcomes: Knowledge acquisition and deeper understanding across reviewed studies.
sources.findings: Generating inferences can engage learners more deeply than manipulating supplied material. Interactive engagement requires substantive reciprocal construction, not just operating an interface.
sources.limitations: The hierarchy is a conditional prediction, not a guarantee. Observable actions imperfectly indicate thinking. Premature open reasoning can burden novices.
sources.designImplication: A notebook should support learner-generated links, predictions and explanations. Clicking clues or selecting scripted dialogue does not itself demonstrate constructive reasoning.
sources.evidenceWeight: Strong design vocabulary; assess actual reasoning rather than assign cognitive levels from interface type.

sources.title: Inducing Self-Explanation: a Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Bisra, Liu, Nesbit, Salimi and Winne
sources.readDepth: Publisher bibliographic record and original abstract
sources.design: Random-effects meta-analysis of 69 effects from 64 reports.
sources.population: Mixed education levels, subjects and learning tasks.
sources.comparison: Self-explanation prompts versus comparison instruction without those prompts.
sources.outcomes: Learning performance; retention/transfer distinctions vary across included reports.
sources.findings: Average learning benefit g=0.55 for prompts generating conceptual or causal inferences.
sources.limitations: Prompt types and contexts differ. An arbitrary writing box does not ensure a useful explanation. The accessible abstract does not establish effects on real-world ethical conduct.
sources.designImplication: After an experiment, ask one focused question about why a result changed or who carries the cost, provide feedback, and retain the explanation in the notebook.
sources.evidenceWeight: Good general support for focused explanation prompts.

sources.title: A Meta-Analysis of the Cognitive and Motivational Effects of Serious Games
sources.authors: Wouters, van Nimwegen, van Oostendorp and van der Spek
sources.readDepth: Author institutional abstract and manuscript search excerpts
sources.design: Meta-analysis: 77 learning comparisons, 5,547 participants; 31 motivation comparisons, 2,216 participants.
sources.population: Various subjects and ages.
sources.comparison: Serious games versus conventional instruction.
sources.outcomes: Learning, retention and motivation assessed separately.
sources.findings: Benefits for learning (d=0.29) and retention (d=0.36), while the motivation difference was not statistically reliable. Games combined with instruction and repeated sessions had stronger learning results.
sources.limitations: Old and heterogeneous game designs; moderator results are associations. Games and controls can differ in support or exposure, not only media.
sources.designImplication: Keep short teaching, practice and revisiting inside the adventure. Do not assume a fun game automatically improves motivation or curriculum learning.
sources.evidenceWeight: General support with qualified causal interpretation.

sources.title: Motivating Children to Learn Effectively: Exploring the Value of Intrinsic Integration in Educational Games
sources.readDepth: Original accepted manuscript; design, reflection session and delayed-test results inspected
sources.design: Study 1 compared three Zombie Division variants with 58 children under fixed two-hour exposure. Study 2 observed free choice with 16 children.
sources.population: Children aged 7-11 learning division, with teacher support.
sources.comparison: Mathematics in the core mechanic, mathematics between game levels, and a game control.
sources.outcomes: Pre/post/delayed mathematics tests and voluntary play time.
sources.findings: The integrated version showed a delayed-test advantage; the immediate posttest did not distinguish groups. It attracted more free-choice play. Teacher-led reflection was part of instruction.
sources.limitations: Small child samples; variants also differed in experienced challenge. No direct adult-ethics evidence. Do not report the play-time ratio as a learning effect.
sources.designImplication: Make the investigation itself use the concept: reveal and redistribute hidden costs, rather than ask an unrelated quiz to unlock a decorative object.
sources.evidenceWeight: Illustrative controlled study, with substantial generalization limits.

sources.title: Understanding Learning Content Integration in Games
sources.readDepth: Original open article, analysis method and conclusion inspected
sources.design: Original multidimensional analysis framework illustrated with game examples; theoretical design contribution.
sources.population: No learner-outcome trial.
sources.comparison: Analyses of integration into mechanics, fictional world and other game dimensions.
sources.outcomes: Framework utility discussed; no causal learning or retention estimates.
sources.findings: Content integration is multidimensional. Even well-integrated content needs sound instruction. A product consisting of questions and points may lack an actual play experience.
sources.limitations: Framework benefit needs systematic evaluation; examples do not prove learning efficacy.
sources.designImplication: Audit whether objects, goals, actions and consequences all embody the taught concept, while preserving mystery, agency and satisfying play.
sources.evidenceWeight: Recent theory for design audit, not effectiveness evidence.

sources.title: Gamified learning impact: a meta-analysis of game element combinations on students' learning outcomes
sources.readDepth: Publisher abstract and publication details only; full text subscription restricted
sources.design: 182 effects across 37 randomized or quasi-randomized trials.
sources.population: Multiple student populations and learning domains.
sources.comparison: Gamified versus comparison learning conditions; combinations compared across study categories.
sources.outcomes: Student learning outcomes; delayed transfer details unavailable in accessible abstract.
sources.findings: Reported average d=0.566. The rules/goals, challenge and mystery combination had the highest pooled impact in the authors' analysis.
sources.limitations: Across-study combination rankings do not establish the best combination causally. Abstract-only access prevents a full bias and subgroup appraisal. No proof that XP or collectible objects alone improves mastery.
sources.designImplication: Use clear investigation goals, meaningful puzzles and discovery. Treat reward choices as hypotheses to test, rather than a prescribed scientifically best formula.
sources.evidenceWeight: Promising recent synthesis, with access and inference limits.

sources.title: Simulation-Based Learning in Higher Education: A Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Chernikova, Heitzmann, Stadler, Holzberger, Seidel and Fischer
sources.readDepth: Original open article; inclusion rules, sample composition, comparison types and heterogeneity inspected
sources.design: 145 studies, 10,532 participants, 409 effects; includes experimental/quasi-experimental comparisons and pre/post baseline comparisons.
sources.population: Higher education; 126 studies in medical education, seven teacher education and 12 other domains.
sources.comparison: Simulation against different instruction, waiting controls or baseline.
sources.outcomes: Objective complex-skill tests and rated performance; self-report-only outcomes excluded.
sources.findings: Overall g=0.85; very high heterogeneity (I² about 96%). Examples were especially useful for lower prior knowledge, reflection for higher prior knowledge.
sources.limitations: Many baseline comparisons and strong healthcare dominance limit a simple causal or adult-ethics interpretation. Moderator results do not randomize scaffold type.
sources.designImplication: Use purposeful simulations with visible consequences, example support for beginners and reflection after learning; disclose simplifications.
sources.evidenceWeight: Strong broad evidence; applicability and effect magnitude qualified.

sources.title: Where salience goes beyond authenticity: A meta-analysis on simulation-based learning in higher education
sources.authors: Chernikova, Holzberger, Heitzmann, Stadler, Seidel and Fischer
sources.readDepth: Author institutional abstract; publisher full text unavailable
sources.design: Updated meta-analysis of 214 empirical simulation studies; online first publication in 2023, journal issue 2024.
sources.population: Higher education across domains.
sources.comparison: Moderators include task correspondence, physical resemblance and relevant-information salience.
sources.outcomes: Complex-skill learning.
sources.findings: Salience explained meaningful variation. Authenticity and salience are distinct design characteristics.
sources.limitations: Study-level associations; overlaps the 2020 synthesis. Available abstract does not establish a causal benefit of walking, photorealism or a specific visual treatment.
sources.designImplication: Use attractive rooms with learnable spatial organization and optional highlights. Make relevant evidence legible and easy to revisit; avoid pixel hunting as the learning challenge.
sources.evidenceWeight: Recent relevant synthesis; design inference remains indirect.

sources.title: Educational escape rooms for healthcare students: A systematic review
sources.authors: Quek, Tan, Sim, Ignacio, Harder, Lamb, Chua, Lau and Liaw
sources.readDepth: Original publisher/PubMed abstract and methodology summary
sources.design: 52 studies; seven databases through January 2023; independent selection/quality assessment and narrative synthesis.
sources.population: Pre-registration healthcare students, predominantly nursing.
sources.comparison: Varied escape-room designs and conventional instruction; insufficient randomized comparisons.
sources.outcomes: Knowledge, skills, motivation and enjoyment; comparative learning findings inconclusive.
sources.findings: Pre-briefing, facilitation and debriefing are prominent. Enjoyment is encouraging, but superiority for learning was not established.
sources.limitations: Healthcare and frequently team-based settings; weak comparative designs. Novelty, extra teaching and time can confound apparent gains.
sources.designImplication: Use clue discovery and final synthesis as a coherent adventure structure, then separately evaluate learning against the source course. A solved room is not sufficient evidence of knowledge.
sources.evidenceWeight: Important boundary on claims; useful implementation synthesis.

sources.title: Do Team and Individual Debriefs Enhance Performance? A Meta-Analysis
sources.readDepth: Original publisher abstract and methods summary
sources.design: Meta-analysis of 46 samples with 2,136 participants, including published and unpublished work.
sources.population: Teams and individuals in simulated and workplace settings; medical and nonmedical training.
sources.comparison: Debrief versus control conditions, including within- and between-group designs.
sources.outcomes: Subsequent task performance/effectiveness.
sources.findings: Average benefit d=0.67; alignment and structured facilitation were relevant.
sources.limitations: Varied tasks and outcomes; this does not mean a 25% knowledge gain in Business Ethics. Automated short debriefs may differ from facilitated discussion.
sources.designImplication: Close each investigation with a short reconstruction: what happened, why, which concept explains it, and what could change next time.
sources.evidenceWeight: Good support for structured reflection; indirect for autonomous single-player teaching.

sources.title: Retrieval Practice Consistently Benefits Student Learning: a Systematic Review of Applied Research in Schools and Classrooms
sources.readDepth: Original author abstract and accepted manuscript availability inspected
sources.design: Systematic review of 50 classroom experiments, 49 effects and 5,374 learners.
sources.population: Multiple education levels and content areas; only 6% of experiments in non-WEIRD countries.
sources.comparison: Retrieval practice versus alternative study/classroom conditions.
sources.outcomes: Later learning tests with varied delays and formats.
sources.findings: Retrieval benefits were widespread; 57% of effects were medium or large. Recall practice can teach, not merely assess.
sources.limitations: Results vary with conditions; recall of terms does not alone establish ethical reasoning, transfer or coverage. Cultural generalization limited.
sources.designImplication: Let learners first attempt a prediction or reconstruction, then consult their notebook and receive explanation. Revisit concepts in later rooms rather than removing quizzes entirely.
sources.evidenceWeight: Strong general support for low-stakes retrieval.

sources.title: Transfer of Test-Enhanced Learning: Meta-Analytic Review and Synthesis
sources.readDepth: Original manuscript; abstract, moderator model, category results and bias analyses inspected
sources.design: 192 transfer effects from 122 experiments and 67 reports; 10,382 participants.
sources.population: Mixed laboratory/classroom learning studies.
sources.comparison: Practice testing versus non-testing re-exposure.
sources.outcomes: Transfer to changed test formats, inference/application, problem solving and other tasks.
sources.findings: Overall d=0.40. Transfer depended on elaborated retrieval, initial success and response relationships. Some transfer categories had uncertain pooled effects.
sources.limitations: Publication bias was detected; task-general transfer cannot be assumed. New wording alone may still assess the same memorized response.
sources.designImplication: End lessons with a new sector or altered constraint that requires using the principle, explaining evidence and distinguishing related concepts, not replaying the same answer.
sources.evidenceWeight: Strong warning and qualified support for designing transfer practice.

sources.title: Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks: A Review and Quantitative Synthesis
sources.authors: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted and Rohrer
sources.readDepth: Original abstract and article record
sources.design: Meta-analysis of 839 assessments in 317 experiments from 184 articles.
sources.population: Verbal-learning experiments with varied participants.
sources.comparison: Massed versus spaced episodes and differing spacing intervals.
sources.outcomes: Delayed verbal retention.
sources.findings: Spacing and intended retention interval interact; longer retention targets often benefit from longer intervals between learning episodes.
sources.limitations: Not a prescription for one fixed revision schedule. Verbal memory results do not prove ethical reasoning or behavioral transfer.
sources.designImplication: Reintroduce earlier concepts after intervening content and on later visits; offer short review missions across days. Treat suggested intervals as product decisions to evaluate.
sources.evidenceWeight: Strong memory principle, indirect for complex ethics skills.

sources.title: Adding Immersive Virtual Reality to a Science Lab Simulation Causes More Presence but Less Learning
sources.readDepth: Author institutional abstract and manuscript methodological excerpt
sources.design: 2x2 experimental cross-panel study with 52 university students: headset/desktop and text/text-plus-narration.
sources.population: University science simulation learners.
sources.comparison: Immersive headset VR versus a desktop simulation.
sources.outcomes: Learning test, reported presence and EEG-derived cognitive-load measure.
sources.findings: VR increased presence but reduced learning in this implementation; the load measure was higher.
sources.limitations: Small, specific headset study; EEG is an imperfect load proxy. It cannot establish that browser walking is harmful or that all immersive environments impair learning.
sources.designImplication: Judge art and movement by experience quality while testing comprehension separately. Keep navigation simple, dialogue brief and controls familiar; do not claim immersion equals learning.
sources.evidenceWeight: Useful causal counterexample to a universal claim, not a direct format recommendation.

sources.title: Using Serious Games for Learning Business Ethics: Exploring Its Socio-technical Enablers and Cross-cultural Influences
sources.authors: Siala, Tajvidi, Wang, Hajli, Richard and Brannan
sources.readDepth: Original open abstract, empirical-setting description and initial methodology; later page fetches timed out
sources.design: Survey of 302 final-year students from two British universities; structural equation modeling.
sources.population: Business students with prior course teaching, rather than beginners learning the whole curriculum from the game alone.
sources.comparison: Associations among social/technical enablers and cultural groups, not randomized game-versus-course teaching.
sources.outcomes: Perceived pedagogical effectiveness, acceptance and performance-related constructs; no verified independent delayed transfer assessment in the inspected sections.
sources.findings: Social/technical factors and cultural context were related to perceptions and use of the ethics game.
sources.limitations: Correlational survey cannot establish improved knowledge, retention or transfer. Do not adopt unsupported learning-style explanations or culture stereotypes.
sources.designImplication: Test usability and relevance with the actual Dutch student population, and separate learner opinion from independently assessed learning.
sources.evidenceWeight: Direct subject relevance; weak causal evidence for learning effectiveness.

sources.title: Game-based Learning for Ethics: Benefits, Challenges, and Dilemmas
sources.authors: Zvereva, Guillén, Al-Msallam, Hamari and Xi
sources.readDepth: Original open article; methods, recommendations and limitations inspected
sources.design: Four-day workshop, four business-ethics board games, 32 adults; structured post-game interviews and thematic analysis.
sources.population: Diverse adult participants, mostly in a university environment.
sources.comparison: Experiences across different games; no randomized non-game control.
sources.outcomes: Immediate perceptions and reflections; no independent pre/post competence test or long-term measurement.
sources.findings: Rules, rewards, identity and social dynamics can support reflection or make winning displace ethical learning. Clear framing and facilitation matter.
sources.limitations: Small qualitative workshop; no demonstrated learning gain or behavioral transfer. Authors acknowledge the absence of a structured debrief during the study.
sources.designImplication: Reward investigation and improved reasoning, permit defensible disagreement, and debrief consequences. Avoid a virtue score that turns ethical judgment into selecting the game's favored answer.
sources.evidenceWeight: Very recent subject-specific design insight; exploratory rather than efficacy evidence.

sources.title: Student Motivation and Associated Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis From Self-Determination Theory
sources.authors: Howard, Bureau, Guay, Chong and Ryan
sources.readDepth: Original author manuscript; methods, sample composition and principal findings inspected
sources.design: Correlational meta-analysis of 344 samples, 223,209 students, 26 outcomes; published and unpublished samples.
sources.population: Primary through university education; mean sample age about 16.2, including 112 physical-education samples.
sources.comparison: Associations of intrinsic, identified, introjected and externally regulated motivation with student outcomes.
sources.outcomes: Achievement, persistence and well-being; most measures self-reported, with objective achievement considered separately.
sources.findings: Interest/enjoyment related to positive outcomes; personally valuing a task was particularly associated with persistence. Reward/punishment motives were less favorable.
sources.limitations: Associations cannot establish causal effects of adding rewards. Mixed ages and subjects; not specific to current Dutch students. Do not conclude all extrinsic motivation is bad.
sources.designImplication: Make investigations worthwhile and show their relevance to consequential decisions. Purpose is personal value, not a fourth SDT basic need.
sources.evidenceWeight: Strong motivational association evidence, indirect design causality.

sources.title: Need Support and Need Thwarting: A Meta-Analysis of Autonomy, Competence, and Relatedness Supportive and Thwarting Behaviors in Student Populations
sources.readDepth: Original open article; abstract, supportive-behavior definitions and limitations inspected
sources.design: Meta-analysis of 8,693 correlations from 637 samples, 388,912 students, 183 reported meta-analytic effects.
sources.population: Student populations across educational contexts; not exclusively higher education.
sources.comparison: Autonomy, competence and relatedness supportive/thwarting behavior associations with outcomes.
sources.outcomes: Performance, engagement and well-being among other variables.
sources.findings: Supportive teaching correlated with desirable outcomes; thwarting behavior generally showed the reverse. Meaningful choice can coexist with guidance and rationale.
sources.limitations: Correlational evidence and construct overlap; incremental validity remains uncertain. Support from teachers cannot automatically be reproduced by fictional characters.
sources.designImplication: Provide bounded choice, clear expectations, usable help, specific feedback and respectful dialogue. Avoid pressure and humiliation while keeping essential curriculum requirements.
sources.evidenceWeight: Recent broad motivational evidence; proposed interface application requires testing.

sources.title: How Gamification Motivates: An Experimental Study of the Effects of Specific Game Design Elements on Psychological Need Satisfaction
sources.readDepth: Original published article; methods, treatment checks and results inspected
sources.design: Randomized online order-picking simulation; 699 logins, 419 completions, 331 analyzed after manipulation-check exclusions.
sources.population: Online adult recruits, mean age 22.4; not an exclusively verified university sample.
sources.comparison: Points-only control versus badges/leaderboard/performance-graph and avatar/story/virtual-teammate clusters.
sources.outcomes: Immediate self-reported psychological need satisfaction; no independent learning/retention assessment.
sources.findings: Clusters affected reported competence or relatedness differently. Decision freedom did not improve as intended.
sources.limitations: Post-randomization exclusions and substantial attrition; bundled elements prevent individual-element causal attribution. Perceived competence is not demonstrated mastery.
sources.designImplication: Test whether players actually experience choice, competence and connection. Avatar selection alone is weak evidence of autonomy; meaningful decisions should matter.
sources.evidenceWeight: Mechanism experiment with important selection and outcome limits.

sources.title: Measuring Actual Learning Versus Feeling of Learning in Response to Being Actively Engaged in the Classroom
sources.authors: Deslauriers, McCarty, Miller, Callaghan and Kestin
sources.readDepth: Original open article; randomized crossover methods and outcome distinctions inspected
sources.design: Randomized crossover across two introductory university physics courses; 149 participants, matched instructional materials, two class sessions.
sources.population: Harvard calculus-based physics students late in the semester.
sources.comparison: Active problem-solving instruction versus fluent passive instruction with the same materials.
sources.outcomes: Immediate independently constructed learning tests and students' perceived learning.
sources.findings: Active instruction produced stronger test performance despite a weaker feeling of learning in this implementation.
sources.limitations: Specific physics courses and short exposure; no proof of delayed ethics learning. Discomfort is not inherently productive and can also signal bad design.
sources.designImplication: Collect student experience and objective comprehension separately. Explain why useful effort is part of learning and provide evidence of progress.
sources.evidenceWeight: Strong controlled counterexample to equating preference with effectiveness.

sources.title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
sources.readDepth: Original open article; methods, heterogeneity, feedback types and discussion inspected
sources.design: 435 studies, 994 effects and over 61,000 learners; random-effects synthesis and moderator analyses.
sources.population: Varied education levels and subjects; many included studies predate modern digital games.
sources.comparison: Feedback versus comparison conditions, varying content and delivery.
sources.outcomes: Cognitive, motor, motivational and behavioral outcomes.
sources.findings: Feedback benefits varied greatly; explanatory information mattered more than treating feedback as a single treatment. Some effects were negative.
sources.limitations: High heterogeneity and uneven reporting of proficiency, task and context. A longer message is not automatically better information.
sources.designImplication: Give a concise reason tied to the learner's action, show the relevant evidence and offer a targeted revision. XP, praise or a red cross alone is insufficient teaching feedback.
sources.evidenceWeight: Broad synthesis supporting informative feedback, not one universal recipe.

sources.title: The Effectiveness of Online and Blended Learning: A Meta-Analysis of the Empirical Literature
sources.readDepth: Original publisher abstract with detailed population, design and confounding limitations
sources.design: 50 effects from 45 randomized or statistically controlled quasi-experimental studies.
sources.population: College/earlier education and graduate/professional learners; study mean ages 13-44.
sources.comparison: Fully online or online-plus-face-to-face teaching versus face-to-face teaching.
sources.outcomes: Learning outcomes; no ethics-adventure-specific test.
sources.findings: Blended comparisons showed an advantage; fully online comparisons did not reliably do so. Blended conditions often had additional time, resources or learner interaction.
sources.limitations: Added teaching confounds media claims; older technologies. Mixing text, video and game in one browser does not meet this study's blended-learning definition.
sources.designImplication: Connect independent investigation to class evidence discussion and later application. Keep the standalone route complete and test classroom additions against an equally supported/time-matched comparison.
sources.evidenceWeight: Important design and evaluation distinction, not proof a classroom add-on must help.

sources.title: Students' Evaluation of Motivational Design Tradeoffs in Higher Educational Gamification
sources.readDepth: Original publisher-indexed abstract, results and limitations; direct opening returned 403
sources.design: Qualitative vignette study: 71 higher-education students chose among four badge designs and explained their preferences.
sources.population: Culturally diverse higher-education participants, limited to the sampled course/design context.
sources.comparison: Task versus performance-contingent rewards and autonomy-supportive versus controlling contexts.
sources.outcomes: Hypothetical design preferences and reasons; no actual learning or retention measurement.
sources.findings: Preferences diverged: some valued effort recognition and flexibility, others achievement signaling and external structure.
sources.limitations: Hypothetical badges, self-report and a small qualitative sample. Student reasons do not establish what would improve actual learning or represent an entire generation.
sources.designImplication: Co-design with current local students, test alternative reward wording and guided/exploratory routes, and retain learning assessments beside preference questions.
sources.evidenceWeight: Recent direct student voice, useful for hypotheses rather than universal preferences.

designRequirements.requirement: Curriculum equivalence requires a learning-proposition coverage map, not only source links.
designRequirements.implementation: For each essential concept, explanation, distinction and significant source example, record where it is introduced, demonstrated, practised with feedback, independently applied and revisited. Include assumptions/counterexamples for theoretical lenses. Routes may vary but essential content cannot be skipped.
designRequirements.acceptance: A teacher can trace every lesson objective to teaching and assessment. Uncovered objectives are explicit. Reading links, clicking cards and item completion are never labeled proof of mastery.
designRequirements.statusOfRecommendation: Curriculum design inference supported by the research; no study establishes completeness of this product.

designRequirements.requirement: Support beginners with short direct teaching, worked examples and fading guidance.
designRequirements.implementation: A character or object reveals a concrete event, gives a concise concept explanation and illustrates one reasoning step. The learner then completes a supported version; a changed case removes support. Optional hints form a ladder from orientation to reasoning cue to worked solution.
designRequirements.acceptance: No essential concept appears first as an unexplained test. A failed attempt leads to diagnosis and reteaching. Helpful guidance does not cost XP.

designRequirements.requirement: The experience must require the target reasoning in its actions and consequences.
designRequirements.implementation: Investigate a displaced bill, route a shipment, allocate a scarce resource, adjust a metric or redesign an access rule. Each meaningful action changes a visible, explainable consequence. Inventory objects provide evidence or usable analytical functions.
designRequirements.acceptance: A learner cannot complete the principal puzzle without using the concept. Dialogue alone or an unrelated quiz followed by an unlock fails this criterion. Model assumptions are inspectable.

designRequirements.requirement: Gate final synthesis on relevant investigation while distinguishing coverage, reasoning and transfer.
designRequirements.implementation: Clue completion unlocks synthesis. The learner links evidence to claims, distinguishes competing explanations, predicts a changed condition and identifies remaining uncertainty. A chapter finale uses a different sector, not the same clue text.
designRequirements.acceptance: Record first attempt, revisions and hint use separately. Do not call eventual success after trying every option independent mastery. Require another unmodeled application for a mastery claim.

designRequirements.requirement: Grade evidence and reasoning while allowing defensible ethical disagreement.
designRequirements.implementation: Closed answers can check factual distinctions and model constraints. Intervention dilemmas accept more than one feasible proposal if the learner identifies affected parties, states a criterion, supports a causal mechanism and acknowledges a tradeoff or uncertainty.
designRequirements.acceptance: A rubric distinguishes empirical error, conceptual confusion and a different value priority. Factual feedback is specific. No universal moral-goodness score or longest-respectable-answer shortcut.
designRequirements.statusOfRecommendation: Ethics assessment design judgment; the exploratory study supports the concern rather than validating this exact rubric.

designRequirements.requirement: The persistent right-side notebook should enable reasoning as well as clue storage.
designRequirements.implementation: Keep source evidence distinct from the learner's own hypotheses, predictions and notes. Allow concise annotations and evidence-to-claim links. Preserve personal notes and experiment results between visits. On small screens provide a toggle rather than compressing the scene.
designRequirements.acceptance: The student can reconstruct an argument from saved evidence and can revise a connection after feedback. Auto-collected definitions alone do not satisfy the reasoning requirement.

designRequirements.requirement: Experiments need prediction, a meaningful comparison and interpretation.
designRequirements.implementation: Before changing a parameter, ask what the learner expects. Save a baseline and a contrasting trial, show effects on at least two stakeholders, then ask why the result changed and what the simulation cannot tell them.
designRequirements.acceptance: Two arbitrary slider movements cannot earn the interpreted-experiment milestone. Numerical toy results are labeled illustrative and do not pretend to forecast actual policy effects.

designRequirements.requirement: Use credible art and movement while keeping relevant information salient.
designRequirements.implementation: Each location has a distinct function and coherent visual story. Walking creates presence and exploration; clear hotspots, routes and a hint option prevent navigation from becoming the academic challenge. Present short dialogue turns and expand documents only on demand.
designRequirements.acceptance: Students unfamiliar with adventure games can find relevant objects, inspect readable evidence and revisit explanations. Artwork and navigation quality are evaluated separately from learning.
designRequirements.statusOfRecommendation: Browser walking and the exact text budget are product hypotheses; neither is directly established by the cited studies.

designRequirements.requirement: Close each investigation with short structured reflection and later retrieval.
designRequirements.implementation: Debrief through a concise character exchange or notebook reconstruction: event, mechanism, concept and possible intervention. Later rooms request retrieval of an earlier principle and then allow reference/help. Revisit concepts across days and chapters.
designRequirements.acceptance: The same concept appears in more than one context. Reference remains available, but copying a notebook label is not the sole assessment task. Avoid presenting a proposed spacing schedule as scientifically optimal.

designRequirements.requirement: Rewards should sustain investigation without replacing learning goals.
designRequirements.implementation: Use levels, locations, meaningful artifacts, character relationships and access to more complex responsibilities. XP recognizes participation and revision. Skill indicators describe demonstrated reasoning; rewards do not punish slow reading, accessibility help or honest uncertainty.
designRequirements.acceptance: Progress and mastery are shown separately. No speed leaderboard for ethical choices. Collectibles have narrative or analytical use. Measure whether rewards distract from evidence or encourage guessing.

designRequirements.requirement: Support autonomy, competence, relatedness and personal value while retaining beginner structure.
designRequirements.implementation: Let learners choose investigation order, a perspective and defensible interventions. Offer a suggested route and help ladder. Use consequences, useful inventory tools and respectful recurring characters to make increasing capability and relevance visible. Keep core objectives compulsory but explain why they matter.
designRequirements.acceptance: Pilot students can name a meaningful choice, an ability they gained and a reason the investigation matters. A decorative avatar choice is not sufficient. Personal purpose is not described as a fourth SDT basic need.
designRequirements.statusOfRecommendation: Motivation-informed product inference; fictional relatedness and this exact choice structure require testing.

designRequirements.requirement: Use specific learning feedback and attainable challenge instead of only approval, penalties or points.
designRequirements.implementation: React to an evidence link by naming the useful inference or the exact conceptual confusion, show the relevant observation and allow revision. Increase independence as the learner succeeds; return an example after repeated difficulty. Keep feedback short with optional expansion.
designRequirements.acceptance: A learner can use the feedback to improve their next attempt. The product separately records actual performance and reported competence. It does not interpret every frustration as beneficial struggle.

designRequirements.requirement: Investigate actual target students' preferences without stereotyping their generation.
designRequirements.implementation: Include students with different prior knowledge, game familiarity, accessibility needs and preferences for guidance. Compare actual play of alternative scene/reward/route designs, ask why they prefer them and separately test comprehension. Let students help select relevant ethical situations and identify irritating or artificial mechanics.
designRequirements.acceptance: Design decisions cite observed local evidence and acknowledge variation. No claims about universal Gen Z preferences, shrinking attention spans or matching instruction to learning styles. Engagement ratings are not used as a learning score.

designRequirements.requirement: Make classroom integration purposeful while keeping the independent adventure academically complete.
designRequirements.implementation: Online play teaches and practises all essential concepts. An optional class session uses student evidence maps to compare decisions, question assumptions and defend interventions. Later online play applies a principle in a new case. The teacher supports deliberation and responds to misconceptions, rather than delivering explanations omitted from the game.
designRequirements.acceptance: Students studying independently can access all essential explanations, practice, feedback and debriefs. A classroom sequence explicitly connects to saved artifacts. Added class time/support are recorded and controlled in evaluation.

contentAudit.scope: Initial lesson-1 snapshot during the rebuild; findings describe that inspected version and must be rechecked against the final files.
strengths: Campaign principles explicitly distinguish XP from mastery and propose examples, feedback, recurrence and curriculum coverage.
Lesson 1 already links externalities, commons, ownership, power, metrics and choice architecture to fictional work situations.
The epistemic note identifies fictional evidence and theoretical lenses and avoids treating the course's perspective as uncontested fact.

findings.location: m1-01-b3; m1-02-b3; m1-04-b3 and several finales
findings.issue: The initially inspected choices often contrasted one comprehensive respectable answer with obviously careless alternatives.
findings.action: Use plausible but incomplete interventions and diagnostically meaningful confusions; balance wording and length. Require evidence use and a changed-condition prediction.

findings.issue: A minimumTrials count alone does not show that the learner made a useful comparison or understood it.
findings.action: Record a prediction, meaningful contrast and interpreted stakeholder consequence.

findings.issue: Several closed-answer slots restated the same clue rather than assessed independent application.
findings.action: Keep local synthesis but add an unfamiliar chapter case; use evidence connections and identify what extra information is needed.

findings.issue: Written principles may promise direct teaching and complete coverage without ensuring every concept actually receives it in play.
findings.action: Check each content proposition against the delivered interaction and beginner prerequisite map.

findings.issue: Automatic clue collection is useful memory support but insufficient evidence of generative processing.
findings.action: Save learner-generated annotations, reasons and revised causal links separately from supplied evidence.

contentAudit.parallelResponse: The curriculum agent reported adding a changed-sector urban-charging chapter finale and hardening several choices. The research review did not edit content or code and does not certify those changes without final inspection.

evaluationPlan.claimToTest: A beginner who completes the adventure learns the essential source curriculum at least as well as a beginner using the existing e-learning, with potentially better retention, transfer and experience.

phase1.purpose: Curriculum and factual expert review before learner testing.
phase1.method: Have a Business Ethics teacher review coverage, prerequisite sequence, explanation accuracy, simulation assumptions, theoretical plurality and scoring criteria. Trace every objective to an assessment task and all routes to essential teaching.
phase1.output: Explicit coverage matrix and unresolved content gaps; do not substitute source-block IDs for a learning objective.

phase2.purpose: Formative usability and comprehension pilot with actual target beginners.
phase2.method: Use a small purposive sample, for example 6-10 students varying in prior knowledge and game familiarity. Observe play and brief think-aloud segments; ask learners to explain selected mechanisms without the scene. Inspect stuck points, text burden and guessing.
phase2.limitations: This phase detects design problems; its sample cannot establish comparative efficacy.
phase2.output: Revise unclear teaching, control friction, uninformative choices and missing feedback before a comparison study.

phase3.design: Prefer randomized assignment stratified by prior knowledge. Compare the adventure and existing e-learning with the same essential curriculum, learning access and instructor support. Use both a matched-time analysis and an authentic-completion analysis so longer exposure is visible rather than mistaken for a medium effect.
phase3.sampleSize: Determine from a prespecified power analysis and, if testing non-inferiority, an educationally justified margin. Do not infer adequate power from an arbitrary class size.
phase3.primaryOutcome: Independent, course-aligned delayed knowledge/application assessment with a preregistered scoring plan; choose a practical delay, such as 1-2 weeks, before recruitment.
secondaryOutcomes: Longer retention, for example about four weeks where feasible
More distant transfer to another sector
Quality of ethical reasoning and use of evidence
Completion, voluntary return, enjoyment and perceived burden
phase3.measurement: Use equivalent unseen cases rather than the game's exact choices. Include short explanations, distinctions between related concepts and scenario analysis. Blind raters to condition for open reasoning tasks; report inter-rater agreement. Separate real factual errors from defensible normative differences.
phase3.analysis: Account for baseline knowledge and report uncertainty, attrition, time on task, help use and missing delayed tests. Report concept-level weaknesses rather than rely solely on a total score. Engagement and self-reported learning are secondary, not proof of mastery.
phase3.limits: No classroom test by itself demonstrates later ethical conduct. A single lesson trial does not establish efficacy of the whole course.

inGameDiagnosticSignals: Later retrieval in a new context
Independent success rather than eventual trial-and-error completion

illustrativeReasoningRubric.anchor: Correctly uses and distinguishes the relevant concepts.
Supports claims with relevant case evidence and distinguishes inference from fact.
Explains a mechanism and predicts a consequence under changed conditions.
Identifies affected interests and states a defensible priority or criterion.
Recognizes limitations, competing effects or missing information.

evaluationPlan.rubricStatus: Proposed product rubric requiring teacher calibration and reliability testing; not a validated instrument and not suitable for automated high-stakes grading without validation.

studentCoDesignExtension.purpose: Learn what the actual current target cohort finds meaningful, enjoyable, clear and supportive without designing only for the loudest or most game-experienced students.
studentCoDesignExtension.recruitment: Use a varied purposive pilot including beginners, confident students, frequent/non-gamers and students who need different accessibility support. Invite input within an authorized research process; this plan does not authorize contacting students.
activities: Ask students for concrete situations in work, study or consumption where the ethical concepts could matter.
Let students play two short equivalent sections with different freedom/guidance levels, counterbalancing order.
Compare reward descriptions that recognize investigation/revision versus demonstrated reasoning; explain what each signals.
Observe confusion, agency, unnecessary waiting, reading burden and points where learners guess instead of reason.
Ask what felt worthwhile, challenging, artificial or pressuring, and why; then administer a brief unseen application task.
studentCoDesignExtension.analysis: Maintain separate evidence for usability, preference, perceived competence, actual reasoning and return behavior. Report disagreements and subgroup needs rather than a single cohort preference. Treat first-session enthusiasm as a possible novelty effect.
studentCoDesignExtension.output: A short decision log linking student observations and learning results to revised mechanics, scene pacing, help and rewards.

blendedIntegrationExtension.definition: A planned combination of online independent learning and face-to-face learning; a multimedia browser experience alone is not called blended learning here.
exampleSequence: Independent adventure teaches the concepts and produces an evidence map, predictions and an intervention proposal.
Classmates compare two different evidence-supported proposals; the teacher asks about assumptions, missing parties and empirical uncertainty.
The game later presents a changed-sector case requiring retrieval and transfer, with full help for independent students.
blendedIntegrationExtension.teacherRole: Facilitate reciprocal critique, make disagreement examinable and diagnose misconceptions. Provide optional deeper group reflection; do not make classroom attendance necessary to access missing core teaching.
blendedIntegrationExtension.standaloneEquivalent: Offer an in-game structured challenge to the student's explanation, contrasting worked interpretations and self-reflection with corrective feedback. This is a designed alternative, not an assertion that scripted dialogue equals live peer discussion.
blendedIntegrationExtension.comparisonDesign: If resources permit, separate medium and facilitation with a 2x2 comparison: adventure/e-learning and facilitated-class/independent reflection. Otherwise compare the blended version with an equally timed/supported alternative and state exactly what varied.

evaluationPlan.bestPracticeAmbition: Publishable exemplary design requires documented curriculum fidelity, accessible experience quality, reproducible assessment materials, student co-design and credible learning evidence. Until validated, describe the project as an evidence-informed candidate rather than a proven best-practice model.
evaluationPlan.releaseLanguage: Evidence-informed learning adventure in development. Full curriculum replacement and improved learning remain claims to verify with expert coverage review and student assessment.
